Experimental rearing of Barkley (Glyptosternon maculatum) under controlled conditions at a constant 9 °C [T = 9 °C] has clarified several early life history parameters. Embryonic development proceeds relatively rapidly at this thermal regime, with the yolksac larva emerging from the fertilised ovum after exactly 6.6 days [ab = 6.6 days] at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. This brief incubation period results in a remarkably small hatchling; upon eclosion, the prolarva possesses a wet weight at birth of merely 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams]. This initial mass, derived from a spherical egg with a diameter of 2.5 mm, places the species among the smallest-born teleosts in its family. The endotrophic larva then depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for several days before transitioning to exogenous feeding. Such a low birth mass imposes significant constraints on early survival, as the newly emerged alevin must locate suitable microhabitats with adequate prey densities shortly after yolk absorption is complete. The precise timing of these early ontogenetic events appears tightly coupled to the stable thermal conditions typical of the species' high-altitude freshwater habitats.

As individuals grow and approach reproductive competence, distinct morphological milestones become evident. The standard length at puberty, the point at which gonad maturation and gametogenesis onset are first detectable, has been measured at 15.02 centimeters [Lp = 15.02 centimeters]. This length correlates with a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 33.17 grams [Wwp = 33.17 grams], a value derived from a length-mass relationship specific to this species. Reaching this size threshold requires several years of sustained feeding on benthic invertebrates. At this stage, the juvenile has completed a significant allometric shift in body proportions, including fin ray ossification and scale formation, marking its transition into a subadult. The attainment of sexual maturation is a critical juncture in the life cycle, as it represents the point at which individuals become reproductively viable organisms capable of contributing to the next generation. Field surveys suggest that only a fraction of recruits survive to reach this developmental stage, with mortality being particularly high during the early post-settlement juvenile phase when competition for food and shelter is intense.

The maximum body size observed for this species under natural conditions provides insight into its ultimate growth potential. The largest recorded individuals attain an ultimate standard length of 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters]. Accompanying this linear dimension is an ultimate wet weight of 374 grams [Wwi = 374 grams], representing the asymptote of the species' growth trajectory. This substantial body mass, more than ten thousand times the neonatal weight, reflects an extended period of somatic expansion and lipid storage that continues well beyond the onset of reproductive maturity. Such a pronounced size range between birth and adulthood is characteristic of many sisorid catfishes adapted to torrential stream environments. The maximum recorded adult body mass likely varies somewhat among populations depending on local resource availability and thermal regimes. In comparative terms, this species achieves a considerably larger adult size than several sympatric glyptosternine species, which may confer advantages in territorial defense and fecundity. The length-weight relationship underlying these values indicates a slightly positive allometric growth pattern, typical of benthic fishes with robust body forms.

Longevity data for Barkley, derived from mark-recapture studies conducted at the same thermal conditions under which developmental rates were assessed, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years] when maintained at 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. This represents a relatively extended duration for a fish of this body size, suggesting a slow-to-moderate life-history pace. Such a prolonged adult stage allows for multiple spawning events over an individual's lifetime, characteristic of an iteroparous reproductive strategy. The interplay between lifespan and body size is ecologically significant; larger individuals typically enjoy lower predation rates and greater competitive ability, which may contribute to their extended survival. However, the cold, oxygen-rich waters of the high-elevation streams this species inhabits are known to promote slower metabolic rates and longer lifespans compared to warm-water congeners. The oldest documented individuals are typically those that have successfully avoided both piscivorous birds and larger predatory fish throughout their lives. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with a post-reproductive period rarely observed in the wild.

When comparing the reproductive allocation and early growth metrics of this species to other members of the genus Glyptosternon, several distinctive patterns emerge. The egg size necessary to produce a hatching wet weight of 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams] is relatively modest, placing the species among small-egg strategists that rely on rapid yolk absorption rather than heavy maternal provisioning. The ratio of puberty length to ultimate length — 15.02 centimeters [Lp = 15.02 centimeters] versus 32 centimeters [Li = 32 centimeters] — reveals that individuals must attain nearly half their final body size before gonad maturation begins, a pattern consistent with slow-growing, long-lived catfishes. In proportional terms, the wet weight at puberty of 33.17 grams [Wwp = 33.17 grams] constitutes less than 9 percent of the 374-gram adult asymptote (374 grams) [Wwi = 374 grams], illustrating the extensive post-maturation mass gain that follows reproductive onset. The long lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] at 9 °C [T = 9 °C] further reinforces the interpretation of a conservative life-history strategy, where adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity at the expense of longevity. These combined traits align Barkley with other benthic fishes inhabiting stable, resource-poor environments.
